summary: StellarMind – Mission Commander is a browser-based educational game where students plan a complete space mission from concept to review. Players choose a destination (Moon, Mars, Jupiter or Saturn), define a scientific objective, design a spacecraft, select instruments and a fictional launch vehicle, and plan communications and orbit. A live resource panel shows mass, power, budget and data limits, so users see how one decision affects the whole mission. A six-stage simulator presents decision events, and a transparent rule-based evaluation scores the result and explains what to improve. It makes abstract engineering trade-offs hands-on for beginners.
details:
What it does. StellarMind guides a player through the mission-design process in ten sections: Dashboard, Mission designer, Spacecraft, Instruments, Launch, Comms & Orbit, Simulator, Evaluation, NASA Data and Report.

  • Mission designer: name, destination, scientific objective, mission type, duration and budget.
  • Spacecraft: choice of bus, propulsion, power, thermal control and communication system.
  • Instruments: camera, spectrometer, radar, magnetometer and atmospheric sensor, each with mass, power, data rate, cost and an explanation of how it serves the chosen objective.
  • Launch: three fictional launch vehicles whose capacity depends on destination difficulty.
  • Communication and orbit: a simplified data-capacity estimate and rule-based orbit compatibility checks (low orbit, high orbit, transfer trajectory, flyby).
  • Simulator: six stages (design, launch, cruise, arrival, science operations, review), each with a decision event. Choices change the operations score and cost, and some conditions can end the mission in failure.
  • Evaluation: nine pass/fail constraint checks and a 0–100 score.
  • Report: a mission report that can be copied, downloaded as CSV, or printed/saved as PDF through the browser.
  • Progress and mission history are saved in the browser’s local storage.

How it works. A live panel recalculates spacecraft mass, payload mass, power demand and availability, budget use and communication capacity after every change, and shows warnings when a limit is exceeded. Solar power falls with the inverse square of distance from the Sun, so solar arrays work at the Moon but not at Saturn, which teaches why nuclear power sources are used far from the Sun. The score is the average of seven sub-scores (budget, mass, power, communication, science coverage, orbit, operations) with equal weights. Any hard failure (too heavy to launch, propulsion too weak, orbit not allowed) forces a failure result.

Benefits. Students experience trade-offs such as more instruments meaning more mass, power, cost and data, and can immediately see the consequences. Choices in the simulator are deterministic, so users can replay and compare strategies.

Honest limitations. This is an educational game, not a flight-certified tool. Part masses, costs, distances, launch vehicles and thresholds are illustrative game assumptions. Launch vehicles are fictional. The communication model is a simplified toy estimate, not a real link budget. Orbit planning is rule-based and does not compute real trajectories. The scoring is a rule-based evaluation engine and not an AI system. The NASA data is a static reference dataset, not a live API.

Tools used. HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript in a single page with no external libraries, the browser Canvas API for the animated starfield, the browser localStorage, the Sora typeface (Google Fonts), and GitHub Pages for hosting.
